displayQuote: If you don't like something, change it. If you can't change it, change your attitude

meta.title: Who really said "If you don't like something, change it. If you can't change it, change your attitude"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The line is genuinely Maya Angelou — but a paraphrase. Her 1993 book says “change the way you think about it,” not “change your attitude.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you don't like something, change it. If you can't change it, change your attitude'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely rooted in Maya Angelou's 1993 book — but the popular wording is a paraphrase, not her verbatim words.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Maya Angelou and genuinely rooted in her writing: her 1993 essay collection ‘Wouldn’t Take Nothing for My Journey Now’ contains “What you’re supposed to do when you don’t like a thing is change it. If you can’t change it, change the way you think about it.” The crisp popular wording — with ‘change your attitude’ — is a paraphrase, not a sentence found verbatim in any primary source.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

source.excerpt: So you watch yourself about complaining, Sister. What you’re supposed to do when you don’t like a thing is change it. If you can’t change it, change the way you think about it. Don’t complain.
trail: The verbatim passage — “change the way you think about it” — is documented from ‘Wouldn’t Take Nothing for My Journey Now’ (1993) on Goodreads ↗.
The paraphrased popular form (“change your attitude”) circulates as an Angelou quotation with no source cited — see the community-added entry on Goodreads ↗.
Angelou returned to the same idea in ‘Letter to My Daughter’ (2009): “If you cannot make a change, change the way you have been thinking,” as catalogued on Wikiquote ↗.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular version compresses this and swaps ‘change the way you think about it’ for ‘change your attitude’
source.excerptNote: In the book the counsel appears in a passage about resisting the habit of complaint; the crisp motivational-poster form circulating online is a later paraphrase of these lines.
source.rightsNote: The underlying text is from a 1993 copyrighted work by Maya Angelou (Random House) and is not in the public domain; quote briefly with attribution.

author.name: Maya Angelou
author.heading: About Maya Angelou
author.bio: Maya Angelou (born Marguerite Annie Johnson, 1928–2014) was an American memoirist, poet, and civil-rights activist, best known for her landmark 1969 autobiography I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings. Her 1993 essay collection Wouldn’t Take Nothing for My Journey Now gathered aphoristic reflections on courage, faith, and living well — among them the counsel against complaining that this quote paraphrases. Angelou’s fame has also made her one of the most misquoted authors online, which makes separating her real words from smoothed paraphrases worthwhile.

misattribution.heading: The wording problem
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the wrong author — the thought is authentically Angelou’s. The catch is the wording: the polished poster version is a paraphrase that drifted from what she actually wrote.

items.why: Angelou’s 1993 book reads “change the way you think about it,” not “change your attitude,” and the compressed one-liner appears in quote databases with no source cited — see the unsourced community entry on Goodreads ↗ versus the sourced book wording here ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the sentiment is genuinely Maya Angelou’s, from ‘Wouldn’t Take Nothing for My Journey Now’ (1993) ↗ — but the crisp “change your attitude” form is a paraphrase, not her verbatim line.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: In Wouldn’t Take Nothing for My Journey Now (1993), Angelou frames the line as hard-won counsel against the corrosive habit of complaint: “So you watch yourself about complaining, Sister. What you’re supposed to do when you don’t like a thing is change it. If you can’t change it, change the way you think about it. Don’t complain.”

Stripped to a two-clause maxim and given the punchier “change your attitude,” it became one of Angelou’s most-shared motivational lines — which is exactly how the paraphrase hardened into ‘the quote.’
detailsBody: Because a real, published Angelou passage plainly underlies the line, this is not a misattribution to the wrong person — it is genuinely hers in substance. It is filed as attributed rather than verified only because the specific words people quote (“change your attitude”) are a paraphrase that does not appear verbatim in any primary source.
context.pull: Change it — or change the way you think about it. Don’t complain.
